Frozen edamame pods work just as well as fresh. Most supermarkets sell them year-round in the freezer aisle. Do not thaw them before cooking. Cook from frozen straight into well-salted boiling water. The cooking time from frozen is 4 to 5 minutes rather than 3 for fresh. They should be bright green and tender, not mushy.

items.prepNote: frozen pods, straight from the freezer

content.text: Fill a large saucepan with plenty of water. Add a generous pinch of salt, about 1 teaspoon per litre. Bring to a rolling boil over a high heat.
Add the frozen edamame pods directly to the boiling water. Do not thaw them first.
Cook for 4 to 5 minutes. Test one pod by squeezing out a bean and tasting it. It should be tender with a slight bite, like a fresh pea. If still hard, cook for another minute.
Drain in a colander. Shake off any excess water.
While still hot, tip the pods into a bowl. Sprinkle with a good pinch of flaky sea salt. Toss to coat. Scatter over the sesame seeds if using.
Serve in the bowl with an empty bowl alongside for the discarded pods. Eat by squeezing the beans out of the pod directly into your mouth.

items.cause: Not enough salt in the cooking water or after draining
items.fix: The water should taste noticeably salty, similar to a mild pasta water. Season again generously as soon as they are drained and still hot so the salt sticks.
Edamame need only 4 to 5 minutes from frozen. Check at 4 minutes. They should have a slight bite. Drain and cool immediately if overcooked to stop carryover cooking.

items.symptom: The beans are difficult to squeeze from the pod
items.cause: Pods are still cold or were undercooked
items.fix: Make sure the pods are cooked all the way through. Serve hot. The warmer the pod, the easier the beans slip out.

content.text: Edamame have been grown in Japan since at least the 11th century. They are a summer crop, harvested when the soybeans are still young and sweet inside the fuzzy green pod. At an izakaya, a cold beer and a bowl of salted edamame is the unofficial opening ritual of the evening. The pods are not eaten, just the beans inside. Japan exports frozen edamame widely, which is why the dish has spread easily to home kitchens in the UK. It is one of the most straightforward Japanese recipes to make and one of the most reliably impressive at any gathering.
